title: 2 Samuel 5:6–16
context: 2 Samuel 5:6–16 describes David’s capture of the Jebusite stronghold of Zion, which becomes David’s city. The Jebusites taunt that even the blind and lame could keep him out. The details of the attack in 5:8, including the word translated "watercourse," are obscure, and interpreters read them in different ways. David builds up the city, Hiram of Tyre supplies cedar and craftsmen for his house, and David recognizes that the LORD has established his kingdom for Israel’s sake. The narrator also records that David took more wives and concubines and lists sons born in Jerusalem, including Nathan and Solomon. Both traditions see the LORD’s presence as the reason for David’s rise, while noting the narrator’s restraint about the additional wives.

verses.text: The king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who spoke to David, saying, “The blind and the lame will keep you out of here,” thinking, “David can’t come in here.”
verses.arminianNotes: David and his men go against the Jebusites in Jerusalem, who taunt that the blind and the lame will keep him out. Arminians see proud confidence in a fortified city, with the Jebusites assuming David cannot take it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the taunt as a boast that the city’s defenses are so strong that even disabled defenders could hold it. Both traditions see the verse setting up the reversal that follows, when David takes the stronghold.

verses.text: Nevertheless David took the stronghold of Zion. This is David’s city.
verses.arminianNotes: Nevertheless David takes the stronghold of Zion, which becomes David’s city. Arminians see the word "nevertheless" marking God’s help overcoming what seemed impossible, and they note the importance of Zion in the rest of Scripture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that Zion becomes the center of God’s rule among his people and later a picture of God’s city (Psalm 2:6; Hebrews 12:22). Both traditions see the capture as a turning point in Israel’s history.

verses.text: David said on that day, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites, let him go up to the watercourse and strike those lame and blind, who are hated by David’s soul.” Therefore they say, “The blind and the lame can’t come into the house.”
verses.arminianNotes: David says whoever strikes the Jebusites should go up by the watercourse to strike "those lame and blind," and a saying arises that the blind and lame cannot come into the house. Arminians note that the Hebrew is obscure and read the line as turning the Jebusites’ taunt back on them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the meaning of the word translated "watercourse" and of the saying are uncertain. Many read the line as referring to the taunting defenders, not to disabled people generally. Both traditions avoid building doctrine on it, and some note David’s later kindness to lame Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9).

verses.text: David lived in the stronghold, and called it David’s city. David built around from Millo and inward.
verses.arminianNotes: David lives in the stronghold, calls it David’s city, and builds around from the Millo inward. Arminians see David settling and strengthening his capital, preparing a place for the kingdom God has given him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The Millo is usually understood as a terraced or filled structure, though its exact nature is uncertain. Both traditions read the verse as recording David’s building, which later becomes the setting for the ark and the temple.

verses.text: David grew greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of Armies, was with him.
verses.arminianNotes: David grew greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of Armies, was with him. Arminians see the LORD’s presence as the reason for David’s success, which David received as he walked with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see this as the key to David’s rise throughout the narrative (1 Samuel 18:14). Both traditions read the title "the God of Armies" as stressing God’s power over all forces, and both see David’s greatness as God’s gift.

verses.text: Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, with cedar trees, carpenters, and masons; and they built David a house.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram of Tyre sends messengers, cedar, carpenters, and masons, and they build David a house. Arminians see foreign rulers recognizing David’s kingdom, a sign that God was establishing him among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Hiram later helps Solomon build the temple (1 Kings 5). Both traditions see the verse as part of God’s blessing on David’s reign, and both note that the house for David comes before the question of a house for the LORD in chapter 7.

verses.text: David perceived that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for his people Israel’s sake.
verses.arminianNotes: David perceives that the LORD has established him as king and exalted his kingdom for Israel’s sake. Arminians see David rightly understanding that his kingship is a trust for the good of the people, not for his own glory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress the phrase "for his people Israel’s sake": the king exists for the sake of God’s people. Both traditions read the verse as a model of humble leadership that acknowledges God as the source of authority.

verses.text: David took more concubines and wives for himself out of Jerusalem, after he had come from Hebron; and more sons and daughters were born to David.
verses.arminianNotes: David took more concubines and wives in Jerusalem, and more children were born. Arminian readers note the narrator’s restraint and many connect the verse with the warning in Deuteronomy 17:17 against kings multiplying wives, which later brought trouble in David’s family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The narrator records the fact without direct comment, but the later conflicts among David’s sons show its cost. Both traditions read the verse as an honest record of a godly king’s weakness, not as approval.

verses.text: These are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
verses.arminianNotes: The sons born in Jerusalem include Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. Arminians note that Solomon, who will succeed David, is listed here among the others without special notice, and they see the list as an honest record of David’s family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that both Solomon and Nathan appear in the genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:6; Luke 3:31). Both traditions see God’s purposes working through David’s line in ways not yet visible in this list.

verses.arminianNotes: The list continues with Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, and Japhia. Arminian readers see the genealogical detail as part of the historical record, showing that David’s household grew significantly during his reign in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 3:5–8 and 14:4–7 has some differences in the names. Both traditions treat the list as historical record and do not build doctrine on the variations.

verses.arminianNotes: The list ends with Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet. Arminians see the record as completing the account of David’s family in Jerusalem, a reminder that God’s promise to David included his household and descendants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the list as preparing for the promise of 2 Samuel 7 concerning David’s offspring. Both traditions read the genealogy as part of the narrative’s attention to David’s house, which becomes central in later chapters.
